title: Comparison with Mulligan's concert band
summary: Kirchner hears Norvo-era charts in Mulligan and Brookmeyer; Sauter recalls a chart for Gerry that was not his style.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It struck me when I heard the things that you did for Red, you're familiar with Gerry Mulligan's concert bands of the early sitties, and it struck me how much the charts that Mulligan and Bob Brookmeyer and Gary McFarland did twenty five years later, how much they sounded like what you had done in the late thirties.

It is the same very light, very woodwindish sort of colorations, a lot of clarinet lead in the reed section, but using the clarinet and the lower and middle registers. There's a lot of similarity, I was surprised by that.
I hadn't thought of that. You're probably right.
Mulligan had three trumpets, three trombones, four saxes and himself playing and then bass and drums and later he had guitar.
He played it once in a while. There was "a" piano player. He would play it once in a while or Brookmeyer would.
Good choice. Brookmeyer is one of my favorites.
I remember that band. I did something I had done for Ray McKenley and reworked it.
I forgot the title; it was one of those that Ray never played.
I took it to Germany with me; there were four of them and I think there are still two I haven't heard.
One of them I did for Gerry and it was not his style either; he didn't want to do it. He put it away and that was it.
We were talking about Norvo's band.
